title: An explicit, checkable counterexample to Hadwiger's conjecture
W: Hadwiger's conjecture says a graph that needs t colours contains the complete graph K_t as a minor. A disproof claimed in October 2026 (not yet peer reviewed) is non-constructive: it uses graphs with no three pairwise non-adjacent vertices, on roughly 2^(10^12) vertices or more, and never names a graph. Find one concrete graph on fewer than a million vertices for which the conjecture fails, with a proof that can be checked.
M: For a finite graph $G$ let $h(G)=\max\{t: K_t\preceq G\}$ be its Hadwiger number and $\chi(G)$ its chromatic number. Exhibit an explicit graph $G$ with $|V(G)|<10^6$ and $h(G)<\chi(G)$, with a complete proof of both bounds that can be checked (by hand or by a computer computation of feasible size). Sufficient route (Cambie): an explicit $G$ with $\alpha(G)\le2$, $|V(G)|=4t-1$ and no connected matching of size $t$ (a matching whose edges are pairwise joined by an edge of $G$) violates Hadwiger's conjecture.
why: Hadwiger's conjecture (1943) is one of the central problems of graph theory, generalizing the Four Colour Theorem; a disproof would reshape the theory of minors and colouring. A non-constructive counterexample of tower-like size tells us little about where the conjecture fails, while an explicit moderate-size one would be checkable, would independently confirm the claim, and would show which structures (e.g. dense graphs with independence number 2, Seymour's test case) actually break it.
issues: Premise checked: the only claimed disproof found is in OpenAI's October 2026 bulk release (Family 157 in the survey arXiv 2610.17090): non-constructive, alpha(G)≤2, m = 2^(1000·g·M0·n) with g = 10^9+1, h(G) < 26m/75 + 2/3; not peer reviewed. The odd, list and dominating Hadwiger variants have separate disproofs, which do not refute the original. The original 'or prove every counterexample is larger' half is hopeless (it would prove HC for all graphs under 10^6 vertices, including χ up to ~10^6) and the 10^6 cutoff is arbitrary, so reframed as an explicit, certified construction. Caveat: if the claimed disproof is wrong, the problem becomes essentially Hadwiger's conjecture itself. Certifying h(G) < χ(G) for a large dense graph is itself nontrivial (Hadwiger number is NP-hard), so the certificate is part of the task. Known: HC holds for t ≤ 6 (Robertson–Seymour–Thomas), so χ(G) ≥ 7 is necessary. | RED TEAM: Premise confirmed: Family 157 of OpenAI's Oct 2026 release, surveyed in arXiv 2610.17090, is non-explicit, not peer reviewed and unverified. M's 'Equivalently decide min<10^6' is false (deciding includes the hopeless negative half), so I removed it. The 10^6 cutoff is arbitrary and the problem rests on an unverified claim. FGS is known for t<=22, so this route needs n>=91. B.

title: Ergodicity of the regular tetrahedron billiard
W: A billiard ball bounces inside a regular tetrahedron. The tetrahedron does not tile space, and its dihedral angle arccos(1/3) is an irrational multiple of pi. So the billiard cannot be unfolded into a straight-line flow on a torus or a translation structure. Is the motion ergodic, so that almost every trajectory equidistributes in position and direction?
M: Let $\Delta\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a regular tetrahedron and $\phi_t$ the billiard flow on the unit tangent bundle $T^1\Delta$, with specular reflection at faces and orbits hitting edges or vertices discarded (a null set). Prove or disprove that $\phi_t$ is ergodic with respect to Liouville measure.
why: Ergodicity of billiards in irrational polygons is open even in the plane. No explicit irrational triangle is known to be ergodic, although Kerckhoff-Masur-Smillie and Vorobets show that generic polygons are. The regular tetrahedron is the most symmetric and canonical non-rational polyhedron, so it is the natural first test case for polyhedral billiards. In that setting the group generated by reflection linear parts is infinite, which rules out the translation-surface methods.
issues: Open as far as I can tell. The literature on tetrahedral billiards covers periodic orbits (Fagnano-type orbits, Bedaride and others) and 'uniformity' results for special polyhedra built from 2D (Beck et al.). I found nothing on ergodicity of the regular tetrahedron. The statement is clean. I added the treatment of singular orbits. Caveat: this is probably far beyond current techniques, since even a single explicit ergodic irrational triangle is unknown. A related, perhaps more tractable variant: is the flow topologically transitive, or are there only countably many periodic directions?

title: Kagome Hofstadter butterfly
W: Electrons hopping on the square lattice in a magnetic field have a Cantor-set spectrum for every irrational flux (the Ten Martini problem, Avila–Jitomirskaya), and the same is now known for the honeycomb lattice of graphene. Prove it for the kagome lattice in a uniform magnetic field.
M: Let $\Lambda$ be the kagome lattice with nearest-neighbour bonds of length $1/2$ (sites $\mathbb Z a_1+\mathbb Z a_2+\{0,a_1/2,a_2/2\}$, $a_1=(1,0)$, $a_2=(\tfrac12,\tfrac{\sqrt3}2)$). For a constant magnetic field $B$ with vector potential $A$, set $(H_B\psi)(x)=\sum_{y\sim x}e^{i\int_{[x,y]}A}\psi(y)$ on $\ell^2(\Lambda)$, and write $2\pi\alpha=B\,|a_1\wedge a_2|$ for the flux per unit cell (so each triangle carries flux $2\pi\alpha/8$ and each hexagon $2\pi\cdot 6\alpha/8$). Prove that $\sigma(H_B)$ is a Cantor set (nonempty, compact, perfect, nowhere dense) for every irrational $\alpha$.
why: Cantor spectrum for the Harper model (Ten Martini, Avila–Jitomirskaya) and for graphene (Becker–Han–Jitomirskaya–Zworski) relied on reducing to scalar quasi-periodic Jacobi operators; the kagome lattice, a line graph of the honeycomb with triangles that pick up flux, does not obviously reduce this way and has a flat band at zero field. A proof would test how far the Ten Martini machinery reaches beyond scalar-reducible lattices, and the kagome butterfly is studied in cold-atom and materials physics.
issues: Original M left the flux distribution unspecified; for a uniform field the triangle flux is 1/8 of the cell flux, so the spectrum is 8-periodic (not 1-periodic) in alpha, and line-graph reductions to honeycomb only work when triangle flux is trivial. Made the Peierls phases explicit. Quick numerics (rational alpha up to 2/5, 3L^2-site tori) show the zero-field flat band at E=-2 disappears for nonzero flux, so there is no isolated infinitely degenerate eigenvalue spoiling perfection; spectrum shows 3q subbands. Literature: Helffer–Kerdelhué–Royo-Letelier treat Hou's kagome model (Chambers formula, band non-overlap) but no Cantor spectrum result found for kagome.

title: 3-SAT at density 4
W: Give a polynomial-time algorithm that, with probability tending to 1, finds a satisfying assignment of a uniformly random 3-SAT formula with n variables and 4n clauses.
M: Let $\Phi$ be a uniformly random 3-CNF formula with $n$ variables and $m=\lfloor 4n\rfloor$ clauses (independent uniform clauses on 3 distinct variables). Give a (possibly randomized) polynomial-time algorithm that outputs a satisfying assignment of $\Phi$ with probability $1-o(1)$. Note that this would in particular prove $r_3\ge 4$ for the satisfiability threshold, whereas the best rigorous lower bound is $r_3\ge 3.52$.
why: Random 3-SAT shows a large gap between where efficient algorithms provably succeed (about 3.52) and the conjectured threshold (about 4.267). Survey propagation appears to work up to about 4.2 in experiments, but nothing has been proved. Closing even part of this gap for k=3 would be a major advance on the 'statistical vs computational gap' programme.
issues: Not novel: the algorithmic gap for random 3-SAT is a well-known open problem, and 4.0 is an arbitrary point inside it. Note the hidden strength. Satisfiability at density 4 is not even proven (best rigorous lower bound 3.52, Kaporis-Kirousis-Lalas and Hajiaghayi-Sorkin; upper bound about 4.49), so a solution would also improve the threshold lower bound. I made the model explicit. A more natural version asks for the largest density reachable by some provable polynomial-time algorithm, or for a proof that survey-propagation-guided decimation works at a given density.

title: How nearly can tetrahedra close up
W: A chain of regular tetrahedra glued face to face can never close up exactly (Świerczkowski). How fast can near-misses improve as the chain grows? Simple arguments show the best gap shrinks at least like 3^{-n/12} and at most like 3^{-n}. A counting heuristic predicts exactly 3^{-n/6}.
M: Let $T_0$ be a regular tetrahedron with edge $2\sqrt2$. A chain of length $n$ is $T_0,\dots,T_n$, where $T_{k+1}$ is the reflection of $T_k$ in a face of $T_k$, and that face is not the one shared with $T_{k-1}$. Let $g(n)=\min_{\text{chains}}d_H(T_n,T_0)$ (always positive). Known or easy: $g(n)\ge c\,3^{-n}$, because all vertices lie in $3^{-n}\mathbb Z^3$ when $T_0$ has vertices $(\pm1,\pm1,\pm1)$ with an even number of minus signs. A pigeonhole argument on pairs of half-length chains gives $\liminf\frac1n\log g(n)\le-\frac{\log3}{12}$ along suitable $n$. Determine $\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\log g(n)$ (or the liminf), conjecturally $-\frac{\log 3}{6}$.
why: Steinhaus's tetrahedral-chain problem asks whether a ring can close. It is a concrete free-product subgroup of the isometry group with all entries in Z[1/3]. The rotation parts behave like the Lubotzky–Phillips–Sarnak quaternions of norm 3^n. The near-closure rate is therefore an optimal-approximation question in an S-arithmetic group acting on R^3, combining a Ramanujan-type rotation part with a translation part that behaves like a random walk.
issues: I added the trivial bounds so that the problem has a definite target. I also made 'the exact rate' a conjecture: proving equality with log3/6 needs equidistribution of translations at scale 3^{-n/6} together with a matching Diophantine lower bound, which is probably far out of reach. A realistic target is to improve either bound. The original said the minimum is over chains 'of length n' without fixing the edge length, so I fixed coordinates. Numerics up to n=13 (531441 chains) give best distances of about 0.28–0.34. At these lengths translational spread still dominates, so the data say nothing about the exponent. Literature: my web-search budget ran out before I could search this item. I know of Świerczkowski's non-closure theorem and the Elgersma–Wagon work on near-closing tetrahedral rings from memory only, so a check is still needed for any prior statement of this rate.

title: Largest prime factor of Markov numbers
W: Markov numbers are the numbers appearing in positive integer solutions of x^2+y^2+z^2=3xyz. Show that the largest prime factor of a Markov number tends to infinity. Equivalently, for any finite set of primes, only finitely many Markov numbers are built from those primes alone.
M: Let $\mathcal M=\{m\ge1:\exists\,x,y\in\mathbb Z_{>0},\ x^2+y^2+m^2=3xym\}$ and let $P(m)$ denote the largest prime factor of $m$ (with $P(1)=1$). Prove that $P(m)\to\infty$ as $m\to\infty$ in $\mathcal M$; equivalently, for every finite set $S$ of primes, only finitely many $m\in\mathcal M$ are $S$-units.
why: Corvaja and Zannier used the Subspace Theorem to show that the greatest prime factor of the product xy over Markov pairs tends to infinity. The single-number version is the natural strengthening. It sits next to the uniqueness conjecture, where Markov numbers that are prime powers are already handled, and to recent strong-approximation work on the Markoff surface.
issues: I found no proof. Single branches are easy: for example, the branch of odd-indexed Fibonacci numbers follows from primitive-divisor theorems. The difficulty is uniformity over the whole tree. Counting does not decide it: there are about (log X)^2 Markov numbers up to X but (log X)^{|S|} S-units, so counting rules out nothing once |S|>=2. A computer check of the 576 Markov numbers up to 1e24 found nothing surprising (smallest largest prime factors above 1000: 53, 61, 109, ...). I did not confirm whether Corvaja-Zannier state the single-number case as open, so novelty is uncertain. The M was made explicit (definition of the set, convention P(1)=1).

title: Quintic Szego growth
W: The cubic Szego equation on the circle is completely integrable, and Gerard-Grellier showed that its smooth solutions can have Sobolev norms that are unbounded in time. Decide whether the quintic Szego equation, which is presumably not integrable, also has smooth solutions with unbounded high Sobolev norms.
M: On $L^2_+(\mathbb T)=\{u\in L^2:\hat u(k)=0\ \forall k<0\}$ with Szego projector $\Pi$, consider $i\partial_tu=\Pi(|u|^4u)$, which is globally well posed in $H^s_+$, $s>1/2$, with conserved $\|u\|_{L^2}$, $(Du,u)$ and $\|u\|_{L^6}$. Decide whether there exist $u_0\in C^\infty(\mathbb T)\cap L^2_+$ and $s>1/2$ with $\limsup_{t\to\infty}\|u(t)\|_{H^s}=\infty$.
why: Unbounded Sobolev growth (weak turbulence) is proven almost only for integrable models such as cubic Szego, using their Lax pairs. The quintic Szego equation keeps the same conservation laws and the H^{1/2} bound but loses integrability, so it is a clean model for asking whether turbulent cascades survive without integrable structure, in the spirit of Bourgain's question for NLS.
issues: Statement is well posed after recording the conservation laws and global well-posedness (H^{1/2} conservation plus a Brezis-Gallouet argument, as in the cubic case; worth double-checking). Literature check incomplete: web search budget ran out before I could search for prior work on quintic or higher-power Szego equations, so novelty is uncertain and needs a check. Hard and natural, but likely out of reach as stated.

title: Three identical vortices on a square torus are chaotic
W: On a flat torus, three point vortices with total circulation zero form an integrable system (Stremler-Aref), but for vortices of equal strength even three are believed chaotic, from numerics only. Prove that three identical point vortices on the square torus are not integrable; the same question is open for four.
M: Let $G$ be the Green function of $\mathbb T=\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+i\mathbb Z)$ ($\Delta G=\delta_0-1$) and $H=-\sum_{i<j}G(z_i-z_j)$ on $\{(z_1,\dots,z_N)\in\mathbb T^N: z_i\ne z_j\}$ with symplectic form $\sum_i dx_i\wedge dy_i$. The centre $Z=\sum_i z_i\in\mathbb T$ is conserved; the reduced space $M_N=\{Z=Z_0\}/(\tfrac1N\mathbb Z[i]/\mathbb Z[i])$ is symplectic of dimension $2N-2$. Prove that for $N=3$ the reduced flow on $M_3$ has no real-analytic first integral functionally independent of $H$ (and likewise for $N=4$ on $M_4$).
why: Point-vortex systems are the standard finite-dimensional models of 2D Euler; integrability is classified on the plane, sphere and for zero total circulation on the torus, but for nonzero circulation on the torus the translation momenta do not commute and only N=2 is integrable. Proving non-integrability for N=3 identical vortices would be the first rigorous chaos result for vortex lattices, where only numerics (Borisov-Mamaev-Kilin) exist.
issues: W's premise was false for identical vortices: Stremler-Aref integrability of three vortices in a periodic parallelogram requires zero total circulation; with nonzero total circulation only N=2 is integrable (survey arXiv 2003.00716, Thm 7) and N=3 is numerically nonintegrable (Borisov-Mamaev-Kilin, RCD 2019). Hence the original 'four identical' version skipped the first open case; restated with N=3 as main case. Clarified the reduction: Z in T is a genuine conserved quantity, translation by 1/N-lattice points acts on its level set, reduced dimension 2N-2 (P_x,P_y do not Poisson-commute, so translations remove only one degree of freedom). Also fixed Green-function normalisation (uniform background). Likely approach: Ziglin/Morales-Ramis along a collinear or symmetric invariant family, or Melnikov splitting; technical but feasible.

title: Sharp linear firefighter constant on Z^3
W: On the 3D grid, any finite fire can be contained if the number of firefighters you place grows linearly in time, and sublinear growth fails. Find the exact critical slope.
M: Firefighter game on $\mathbb{Z}^3$ (nearest-neighbour graph): a finite set $X_0$ burns at time 0. At each step $t=1,2,\dots$ one first protects $\lfloor ct\rfloor$ unburnt vertices (permanently), then fire spreads to all unprotected neighbours of burning vertices. Let $c^*=\inf\{c>0:\text{for every finite }X_0\text{ the fire can be contained}\}$. Determine $c^*$, or at least prove $0<c^*<\infty$ with explicit bounds.
why: Develin and Hartke showed that no constant number of firefighters suffices on Z^d for d>=3. Later work established that order t^{d-2} firefighters per step is exactly the right growth rate, which is linear for Z^3. The sharp constant is the natural next question and is tied to discrete isoperimetry of fire fronts.
issues: The original M was ill-posed. From a single vertex, 5 firefighters per step already suffice on Z^3 (Wang-Moeller, with 2d-1 sharp by Develin-Hartke), so the original f(t)/t tends to 0. The right formulation quantifies over all finite outbreaks with rate ct; I rewrote M that way. Known: O(n^{d-2}) suffices (Dyer-Martinez-Pedroza-Thorne), and o(n^{d-2}) fails for polynomial-growth Cayley graphs (arXiv 2002.11205). I found no work on the constant. A scaling heuristic suggests c* is in (0,infinity), but positivity of c* may itself need proof.

title: Integrability of the egg-crate torus
W: Put the surface z = ε sin x sin y over a flat square torus. Show its geodesic flow is never integrable, however small the bumps are.
M: For $\varepsilon>0$ let $g_\varepsilon$ be the metric on $\mathbb T^2=\mathbb R^2/(2\pi\mathbb Z)^2$ induced from the graph $z=\varepsilon\sin x\sin y$, i.e. $g_\varepsilon=dx^2+dy^2+\varepsilon^2(\cos x\sin y\,dx+\sin x\cos y\,dy)^2$. Prove that for every $\varepsilon>0$ the geodesic flow on $T^*\mathbb T^2\setminus0$ has no real-analytic first integral functionally independent of the Hamiltonian (for example, by showing positive topological entropy).
why: Kozlov's theorem rules out first integrals that are analytic in ε for generic trigonometric perturbations of the flat torus. Proving non-integrability at each fixed ε, uniformly down to ε→0, needs control of exponentially small splitting at resonances. This is an explicit test of that gap.
issues: Wrote out the metric explicitly. The ε-analytic (Poincaré–Kozlov) version follows from Kozlov because the Fourier spectrum of the perturbation is not on a line. The fixed-ε statement for all ε>0 seems open but is quite specific. By Paternain/Taimanov, positive topological entropy would be enough.
